title: The Ming Empire in China (1368–1644)
meta: Ebrey and Walthall · Chapter 14 · Opening questions, p. 227
description: The seven opening questions on page 227 of Ebrey and Walthall’s Ming chapter, with answers and evidence from pages 227–246.
overview: The Manchus founded the Qing dynasty in 1644. Historians have often used the preceding Ming period as a starting point for measuring later changes in China. p. 227

sections.title: 1. How did China compare to Western Europe in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries?

body.p: China had prosperous cities and an ocean fleet larger than the European expeditions the authors describe. On p. 227, the lower Yangzi region stands out for its wealth and its educated writers; merchants supported a growing market for plays and fiction. At sea, Zheng He’s first expedition in 1405 sailed with 317 ships. Columbus and Vasco da Gama led smaller expeditions later that century. pp. 227, 232–233

By the sixteenth century the two economies were trading partners. Portuguese merchants gained a base at Macao in 1557. Chinese merchants sold silk and porcelain; silver from mines in Mexico and Peru reached China through Manila. p. 234

sections.title: 2. Had China already begun to fall behind Western Europe in technology, standard of living, or pace of change?

body.p: The chapter gives no basis for saying China was already falling behind across all three measures. In shipbuilding, the Ming fleet drew on centuries of Chinese advances. Officials who opposed the voyages objected to their cost. Ending them tells us how the court spent its money; it does not show that Europeans had overtaken Chinese shipbuilders. pp. 232–233

Living standards and the pace of change need different evidence. Page 227 describes prosperity around the lower Yangzi River and differences in who owned or rented land elsewhere. By 1600 China had more towns, larger cities and many more books in circulation. Those are signs of change within China. The chapter gives no comparable figures for European households or for how quickly European cities grew. pp. 227, 246

sections.title: 3. At the local level, were communities becoming more integrated into the realm as standardizing policies and economic linkages spread?

body.p: Yes. Villages came under common tax rules, and merchants connected them to wider markets. Page 227 introduces both links. A concrete example is the grain tax: the Ming founder made better-off village families collect and deliver their neighbors’ taxes, mostly paid in grain. The court intended the same rules to apply across the empire. Cheap transport by water also let farmers sell crops beyond their own villages. pp. 227, 240

sections.title: 4. Or were they becoming more diverse as the economy developed in different directions in different places?

body.p: Yes. Selling to a wider market gave regions more reason to produce different goods. The lower Yangzi specialized in cotton and silk, coastal Fujian in tobacco and sugar cane, and Jingdezhen in porcelain. A merchant could buy goods from all three places precisely because they made different things. p. 240

Who controlled the land also varied. Page 227 singles out tenant farming, owners who lived away from their land, and powerful groups of relatives descended from a common ancestor. These family groups, called lineages, sometimes held land jointly and used its income for a school or ancestral temple. They were more common in the south than in the north. pp. 227, 240

sections.title: 5. How effective and how adaptable was the government?

body.p: The founder restored peace after the Yuan collapse, but the system depended heavily on the emperor. Page 227 credits the first Ming emperor, Zhu Yuanzhang, with thirty years of stability despite his harsh rule. He abolished the chancellor’s post. Later emperors needed secretaries to help handle the work that now came to the throne. pp. 227, 229–231

The court could reverse a policy that failed. When pirates raided the coast, officials forced coastal residents to move inland to cut off the pirates’ supplies. The raids proved hard to suppress. Efforts against piracy had more success after the government eased restrictions on maritime trade. pp. 234, 245

sections.title: 6. Why did educated men continue to seek office when the government so often treated them poorly?

body.p: A degree could help a man and his family before he ever held office. Page 227 says competition to enter government eventually surpassed even that of the Song dynasty. The lowest Ming degree excused a man from compulsory labor. The highest qualified him for an official appointment. His success brought standing to his relatives, enough that a lineage might pay to educate a promising boy. pp. 227, 234–236

A man could also keep the standing of a former official after leaving court. Some officials who owned enough property retired early and turned to writing local histories or collecting calligraphy. The danger of serving an emperor helps explain why some left; the rewards of earning a degree help explain why so many still competed. pp. 227, 231, 236

sections.title: 7. What was the impact on the educated class of the changes in the examination system and the explosion of printing?

body.p: Exams gave educated men across the empire a common course of study. Candidates read the same Four Books with Zhu Xi’s interpretations and learned the same essay form. Provincial quotas spread opportunity beyond the wealthy lower Yangzi region. Few candidates advanced: the book estimates that only 2–4 percent passed the provincial exam. For many men, studying and sitting for exams became a lifelong occupation. pp. 234–236

Printing widened what an educated person could read and who else could read it. Exam candidates studied classical written Chinese. Publishers also sold reference books, illustrated stories, novels and plays, many written in the language people spoke. A city reader with little classical schooling could enjoy a story without having the education needed to sit an exam. pp. 227, 236, 242–244

readings: Patricia Buckley Ebrey and Anne Walthall, Pre-Modern East Asia: A Cultural, Social, and Political History, vol. I, 3rd ed., chapter 14, “The Ming Empire in China (1368–1644),” pp. 227–246. The seven questions are from printed p. 227; page numbers after each answer refer to the textbook.
